# 17. Isotonic Tree Labels

## Choose the right boundary function

For a vertex `v`, define `F_v(p)` as the minimum cost in `v`'s subtree when
the label of `v` must be at least `p`. This is exactly the information a parent
passes across the subtree boundary.

The useful slope-trick invariant is

```text
F_v(p) = C_v + sum over b in H_v of max(0, p-b),
```

where `H_v` is a min-heap of integer breakpoints. The constant `C_v` is the
unconstrained minimum subtree cost. Every hinge is flat before its breakpoint
and has slope one afterward, so the heap describes the whole convex,
nondecreasing function without storing values for every possible label.

## Derive the heap transition

Suppose the label chosen at `v` is exactly `y`. Before applying its lower bound
`p`, the cost is

```text
G_v(y) = |y-a[v]| + sum F_child(y).
```

Merge all child breakpoint heaps. The absolute-value term has slope `-1`
before `a[v]` and `+1` after it, which is a slope jump of two. Therefore insert
two copies of `a[v]` into the merged heap.

Far to the left, `G_v` has slope `-1`; each sorted breakpoint raises the slope
by one. Let `b` be the smallest breakpoint. Removing this first slope jump
clips the negative part when we form

```text
F_v(p) = min over y >= p of G_v(y).
```

Thus the complete structural transition is:

```text
merge every child heap
push a[v] twice
b = pop minimum
```

What happens to the constant? Because the heap contains two copies of `a[v]`,
we have `b<=a[v]`. Because `b` is the smallest merged breakpoint, every child
hinge is still zero at `b`. Hence

```text
C_v = sum C_child + |b-a[v]|
    = sum C_child + a[v]-b.
```

We may accumulate `a[v]-b` globally while processing vertices bottom-up. At
the root there is no parent lower bound, so `C_root` itself is the answer.

## Merge heaps efficiently

Each subtree heap contains exactly one breakpoint per subtree vertex: child
sizes add, then pushing twice and popping once increases the total by one.
Always keep the largest child heap and insert every element of smaller child
heaps into it. Whenever a breakpoint moves, the size of its containing heap at
least doubles. It therefore moves only `O(log n)` times.

Root the tree iteratively and process the reversed traversal order to avoid
recursion-depth problems on a chain.

## Sample trace

Each leaf with observation zero inserts `0,0`, removes one zero, and leaves
heap `[0]` with cost zero. At the root, merge the two leaf heaps, insert
`10,10`, and remove the minimum zero. The root contributes `10-0=10`, which is
the optimum: label all three vertices zero.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** If every child function has the hinge representation, the stated
merge, double insertion, and minimum removal produce the hinge representation
of `F_v`.

*Proof.* Summing child functions merges their constants and breakpoint
multisets. Adding `|y-a[v]|` contributes initial slope `-1` and a jump of two
at `a[v]`, represented by two copies. Taking the suffix minimum
`min_{y>=p} G_v(y)` replaces every negative slope by zero. Since the initial
slope is exactly `-1`, this removes exactly the first unit breakpoint, the
minimum heap element. All remaining slope jumps are unchanged.

**Lemma 2.** The constant added at vertex `v` is `a[v]-b`, where `b` is the
removed minimum.

*Proof.* The suffix-minimum function is flat at the unconstrained minimum of
`G_v`, first reached at `b`. No child hinge is positive there because `b` is
the smallest merged breakpoint. Also `b<=a[v]` because two copies of `a[v]`
were inserted. Therefore `G_v(b)` exceeds the sum of child constants only by
`|b-a[v]|=a[v]-b`.

**Lemma 3.** After processing `v`, its heap and accumulated subtree constant
represent the exact optimum for every parent lower bound `p`.

*Proof.* Induct on subtree size. Leaves satisfy Lemmas 1 and 2 with no child
heaps. For an internal vertex, the induction hypothesis makes every child
representation exact; Lemmas 1 and 2 then derive the exact representation at
`v`.

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the minimum total deviation over all
isotonic integer labelings.

*Proof.* Lemma 3 applies to the root. With no parent, its label has no lower
bound, so the required value is the unconstrained constant `C_root`, exactly
the accumulated answer. All breakpoints are observed integers, so an integer
minimizer exists.

## Complexity and traps

Small-to-large movement makes each of the `n` breakpoints move `O(log n)`
times, and each heap insertion costs `O(log n)`. The bound is
`O(n log squared n)` time and `O(n)` memory.

The orientation matters: for `parent <= child`, use a **min-heap** and remove
the minimum. Reversing the inequality reverses the slope picture. Insert the
observation twice, not once. Add the removed-breakpoint difference before
discarding it. Do not attempt to store one DP value per possible label; values
range over two billion integers. Test a decreasing chain, an increasing chain,
a star whose children pull the root downward, equal observations, negative
values, and `n=1`.

# 18. Circulation Repair Queries

## Turn changes into a residual path

The supplied flow already obeys every old bound and conserves flow. Build its
residual graph. An old edge `x -> y` contributes `x -> y` when its flow can be
increased, and `y -> x` when its flow can be decreased.

A proposed mandatory unit on `u -> v` removes one unit of balance from `u` and
adds one at `v`. The old edges repair this exactly when one residual unit can
travel from `v` back to `u`. Capacities are integral, so existence of a path is
both necessary and sufficient; the actual path is also a certificate.

All queries use the same original circulation. Compute the transitive closure
of the residual graph once, using bitsets in Python or a Boolean Floyd--Warshall
loop in C++. Then query `(u,v)` is `YES` precisely when `v` reaches `u`.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** Every legal change to the old flow is an integral flow in the
residual graph, and conversely every integral residual flow produces legal old
edge values.

*Proof.* A forward residual unit increases an edge below its upper bound; a
reverse unit decreases an edge above its lower bound. Cancelling opposite
directions gives the converse mapping without crossing either bound.

**Lemma 2.** The enlarged instance is feasible iff the residual graph contains
a path from `v` to `u`.

*Proof.* Sending one unit on the new `u -> v` edge creates surplus at `v` and
deficit at `u`. A residual `v -> u` path repairs both and conserves every
internal vertex. Conversely, any feasible repair decomposes into cycles and a
unit `v -> u` residual flow; its positive support contains such a path.

**Theorem.** The algorithm answers every query correctly.

*Proof.* Transitive closure records exactly the paths characterized by Lemma 2.

## Complexity and traps

Closure costs `O(n^3)` time and `O(n^2)` bits/Booleans; each query is `O(1)`.
Do not rebuild the network per query. A pinned edge contributes no residual
arc, and the direction tested is `v -> u`, opposite the proposed edge.

# 19. Convex Resource Schedule

## Penalize the number of batches

Let `S[i]` be the prefix sum. With a penalty `lambda` per batch, the DP is

```text
dp[i] = min over j<i of dp[j] + (S[i]-S[j])^2 + lambda.
```

Expand the square:

```text
dp[i] = S[i]^2 + lambda
      + min_j ((-2*S[j])*S[i] + dp[j] + S[j]^2).
```

Thus every completed prefix inserts one line, and every next prefix makes one
minimum query. A discrete Li Chao tree over the nondecreasing prefix sums
handles equal sums without division or floating point.

Store `(penalized_cost, batch_count)`. Run once preferring the fewest batches
on cost ties and once preferring the most. As `lambda` increases, optimal batch
counts never increase. Binary-search the largest integer penalty whose
maximum-tie optimum still uses at least `K` batches. Convexity of squared batch
sums (the Monge quadrangle inequality) guarantees that at this breakpoint the
tie interval contains `K`. If its penalized value is `V`, the answer is
`V-lambda*K`.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** A Li Chao query at `S[i]` returns the minimum penalized transition
into prefix `i`, with the requested count tie rule.

*Proof.* Expansion maps every predecessor to exactly one affine function.
Li Chao insertion preserves the best line at every stored coordinate; comparing
the count after equal values extends the same total order to ties.

**Lemma 2.** Optimal batch count is nonincreasing in `lambda`.

*Proof.* For penalties `a<b`, compare optima with counts `x,y`. Adding their
two optimality inequalities cancels original costs and gives
`(b-a)(y-x)<=0`, hence `y<=x`.

**Lemma 3.** At the located breakpoint, `K` lies between the minimum and
maximum optimal counts, and `V-lambda*K` is the exact `K`-batch optimum.

*Proof.* The interval-cost matrix is Monge because prefix sums are ordered and
the square is convex. Therefore optimum costs as a function of batch count are
discrete convex: adjacent differences are monotone integers. Its supporting
line of slope `-lambda` touches a consecutive interval of counts. The binary
search selects the support where that interval crosses `K`. Every touched
count has original value `V-lambda*count`, giving the formula.

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the minimum cost among exactly `K` batches.

*Proof.* Lemma 1 solves each penalized DP; Lemmas 2 and 3 locate and recover the
required cardinality.

## Complexity and traps

One run takes `O(n log n)` time and `O(n)` memory. There are
`O(log(S[n]^2+1))` runs. Treat `K=1` and `K=n` directly. Li Chao children may
be absent during a query; stop at the best line already seen. Counts are part
of comparisons only after costs tie.

# 20. Laminar Assignment

## Share capacity through the laminar tree

Expanding an offer to all descendant leaves can create quadratic many edges.
Keep the tree itself in the flow network:

```text
source -> worker             capacity 1, cost 0
worker -> offered tree node  capacity 1, offer cost
parent -> child              capacity w, cost 0
leaf -> sink                 capacity 1, cost 0
```

A unit entering a tree node can descend to exactly a leaf in its subtree. The
unit capacity into the sink makes leaves distinct. Send `w` units with
successive shortest augmenting paths and reduced-cost potentials.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** Every integral source--sink path represents one legal worker
assignment with the path's offer cost.

*Proof.* The path chooses one worker, one of that worker's offers, then follows
only parent-to-child arcs to a descendant leaf. All later arcs cost zero.

**Lemma 2.** Integral flows of value `w` correspond cost-for-cost to complete
assignments to distinct leaves.

*Proof.* Unit source edges make each worker occur once. Unit leaf-to-sink edges
prevent repeated leaves. Flow decomposition and Lemma 1 give an assignment.
Conversely, route every chosen worker through its offer and the unique tree path
to its leaf; shared tree arcs have capacity `w`.

**Lemma 3.** Successive shortest augmenting paths produce a minimum-cost flow
of each attained value.

*Proof.* Potentials preserve path costs while making every residual reduced
cost nonnegative. Augmenting on a shortest residual path maintains absence of
a negative-cost residual cycle, the optimality certificate for min-cost flow.

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the minimum assignment cost, or
`IMPOSSIBLE` exactly when none exists.

*Proof.* If value `w` is reached, Lemmas 2 and 3 give the optimum assignment.
If the sink is unreachable earlier, no augmenting path exists, so no flow—and
by Lemma 2 no complete assignment—can have larger value.

## Complexity and traps

With `V=n+w+2` and `E=O(n+w+offers)`, the bound is
`O(w E log V)` time and `O(V+E)` memory. Offers enter a tree node, so tree arcs
must point from parent to child. Duplicate offers are harmless. Count leaves
from the given rooted tree, including the root when `n=1`.

# 21. Persistent Text Occurrences

## Two independent orders

All suffixes beginning with pattern `p` form one contiguous suffix-array
interval `[L,R)`, found by two binary searches. Inside that interval, suffixes
are lexicographically ordered, but the query wants starting-position order.

Build persistent segment-tree root `root[i]` from the first `i` suffix-array
entries, inserting each suffix's starting position. Subtracting `root[L]` from
`root[R]` leaves exactly the occurrence positions of `p`. Counts guide a
standard `k`-th descent; insufficient root count means `-1`.

**Correctness.** Suffix-array contiguity puts exactly the matching suffixes in
`[L,R)`. Persistence inserts each such suffix once, so root subtraction gives
their position multiset exactly. At every segment-tree level the left count is
the number of remaining positions in that half; rank subtraction therefore
ends at the `k`-th smallest position.

Building the suffix array and roots takes `O(n log n)` time and memory. A query
takes `O(|p| log n + log n)` with direct comparisons. Watch the upper-bound
comparison: suffix prefixes equal to `p` belong inside the interval.

# 22. Multi-Archive Common Substrings

## Cap every suffix-automaton state

Build a suffix automaton for the first archive. State `v` represents substring
lengths `(len(link[v]), len[v]]`. Scan another archive while maintaining the
longest current automaton match. Record the best length ending in each visited
state, then propagate states from longer to shorter:

```text
best[link[v]] = max(best[link[v]], min(best[v], len(link[v])))
```

The cap is essential: the parent state represents no length above its own
maximum. Maintain `common[v]`, the minimum `best[v]` over all archives. Then
state `v` contributes
`max(0, common[v]-len(link[v]))` distinct common substrings, and the longest
answer is `max common[v]`.

**Correctness.** The online scan finds every match ending at each position.
Suffix-link propagation transfers all suffixes of those matches and no length
outside the parent interval. Thus `best[v]` is the largest represented length
present in one archive; taking minima makes it the largest present everywhere.
Automaton state intervals partition the distinct substrings, proving both the
sum and maximum formulas.

Time is linear in total archive length plus `k` times the automaton size;
memory is linear in the first archive. Reset per-archive `best`, but never reset
the accumulated minima.

# 23. Palindromic Range Census

## Turn discoveries into points

An Eertree creates one node exactly when a distinct palindrome first appears.
When a node of length `d` is created while reading position `e`, its discovery
interval is the fixed point `(start=e-d+1,end=e)`.

Group these points by `end`, and group queries by right endpoint. Sweep `r`
from left to right. Insert every discovery ending at `r` into a Fenwick tree at
its start. For query `[l,r]`, all inserted points already satisfy `end<=r`;
the answer is the number whose start is at least `l`:

```text
inserted_count - fenwick_prefix(l-1).
```

**Correctness.** Eertree node uniqueness gives exactly one point per distinct
palindrome, at its leftmost ending occurrence. At sweep time `r`, precisely
the points satisfying the query's end inequality have been inserted. Fenwick
suffix counting enforces the start inequality, hence counts exactly the wholly
contained discovery intervals.

Eertree construction is `O(n)` and the sweep is `O((n+q) log n)`, using
`O(n+q)` memory. This problem counts first-occurrence certificates, not every
palindromic occurrence and not distinct palindromes of the query substring.

# 24. Lexicographic Substring Laboratory

Map every text position to its suffix-array rank. A wavelet-style range order
structure over that rank array returns the `k`-th and `(k+1)`-th ranks among
positions `[l,r]`; the suffix array maps them back to positions. Their LCP is
the minimum LCP-array entry strictly after the smaller rank through the larger
rank. A Cartesian tree of the LCP array supports this RMQ as an LCA; the
references use the equivalent static RMQ representation.

Suffix ranks totally order exactly the queried suffixes, so range selection
returns the requested neighbors. The standard suffix-array theorem says the
LCP of ranks `a<b` is `min(LCP[a+1..b])`, proving the second output. Construction
is `O(n log n)` here; each selection and LCP query is `O(log n)`. Do not compute
LCP between adjacent global suffixes—the neighbors are adjacent only after the
position restriction.

# 25. Dynamic Pattern Ledger

Build Aho--Corasick and its failure-link tree. Pattern `i` matches while the
automaton is in state `v` exactly when its terminal node is an ancestor of `v`
in that tree. Euler-tour every failure subtree. Activating a terminal performs
a range add on its subtree; a Fenwick difference array makes the active
ancestor count at state `v` a point query. Scan each query text through the
automaton and sum those point values.

The failure-chain property proves that the point value counts exactly the
active patterns ending at the current character. Summing positions counts all
occurrences, including overlaps and duplicate indexed patterns. Total time is
linear in input text plus `O(log states)` per activation and scanned character;
memory is linear in automaton size. Range-add both endpoints, and treat equal
patterns as separate activations of the same terminal.

# 26. Cyclic Match Convolution

Reverse `a` and concatenate `b+b`. For a concrete character `c`, convolution
of their `c`-indicator arrays at coefficient `n-1+d` counts equal concrete
pairs under shift `d`. Sum this for `a,b,c`. One more convolution of
"is concrete" indicators counts positions where both symbols are concrete.
Their difference is exactly the mismatch count; wildcard positions enter
neither mismatch term.

The convolution identity pairs reversed index `n-1-i` with doubled-text index
`i+d`, hence considers precisely `a[i]` and `b[(i+d) mod n]`. Indicator products
count each eligible position once, proving the subtraction formula. Four NTTs
give `O(n log n)` time and `O(n)` memory. Read coefficient `n-1+d`, duplicate
`b` rather than `a`, and never count wildcard--wildcard as a concrete match.

# 27. Distinct Substring Rank

## Rank blocks in suffix-array order

Sort the suffixes. Suffix `sa[i]` shares its first `lcp[i]` letters with the
previous suffix, so it contributes exactly the new distinct substrings of
lengths `lcp[i]+1, ..., n-sa[i]`, and they come after every substring from
earlier suffixes in lexicographic order. Prefix sums of these block sizes
locate the `k`-th substring by binary search: its block `i` and its length
`len = lcp[i] + (k - before)`.

Its occurrences are the suffixes `sa[i..hi]`, where `hi` is the last index
whose `lcp` values after `i` stay `>= len`. (The block of `i` starts the
interval because `lcp[i] < len`.) Sparse tables on `lcp` and on `sa` give `hi`
by binary search and the leftmost start as a range minimum.

**Correctness.** Distinct substrings are exactly the prefixes of suffixes,
and each is attributed to the first suffix in sorted order that has it as a
prefix. That suffix is `sa[i]` iff the length exceeds `lcp[i]`, so the blocks
partition the substrings in lexicographic order. The occurrence interval
follows from the fact that the LCP of two suffixes is the minimum `lcp` value
between their positions.

**Complexity and traps.** The suffix array costs `O(n log^2 n)` with
comparison doubling, and each query costs `O(log n)`. Printing the substring
itself would be up to `|s|` characters per query, so the statement asks for
`start length` of the leftmost occurrence instead. Ranks reach
`n(n+1)/2 ~ 2 * 10^10`, and `k` up to `10^18` must print `-1`.

# 28. Suffix Pair Affinity

Adjacent suffix-array ranks form edges weighted by their LCP. For any two
ranks, their suffix LCP is the minimum edge weight on the interval between
them. Process these edges from largest weight downward with DSU. When an edge
of weight `w` joins components of sizes `a,b`, exactly `a*b` previously
separate suffix pairs acquire bottleneck—and hence LCP—`w`; add `w*a*b`.

This is the descending-edge construction of the LCP Cartesian/reconstruction
tree. The interval-minimum theorem proves every suffix pair joins at exactly
its LCP value, once, so all contributions sum to the requested aggregate.
After suffix-array construction the scan is `O(n log n)` for sorting (or linear
with bucketed LCPs) and near-linear DSU time. Zero-weight merges contribute
nothing but remain safe.

# 29. Editable Palindrome Rope

Store the string in an implicit randomized treap. Each node maintains subtree
size, forward and backward polynomial hashes under two moduli, plus a lazy
reversal flag. Splitting by size isolates any interval. `REV` swaps children
and the two hash directions lazily; `SET` changes the isolated one-node value;
`PAL` compares its forward and backward hash pairs. Merge the three pieces
after every operation.

Induction on the pull formula shows each aggregate is exactly the polynomial
hash of its in-order string. Lazy reversal preserves that invariant by swapping
directions and child order. Splits preserve in-order sequence, so each command
acts on exactly `[l,r]`. Expected time is `O(log n)` per operation and memory is
`O(n)`. Push reversal before descending, precompute powers through `n`, and
pull after both pointer and character changes.

# 30. Forbidden Superstring Count

Build one Aho--Corasick automaton for every pattern. Propagate a forbidden flag
and a bitmask of required patterns through failure links. For subset `T` of
required patterns, delete states matching a base-forbidden pattern or any
pattern in `T`. Matrix exponentiation of the remaining transition graph counts
length-`L` strings avoiding all those patterns.

Inclusion--exclusion gives

```text
sum over T subset required of (-1)^|T| * avoid(forbidden union T).
```

A walk from the root corresponds bijectively to an alphabet string, and it
survives exactly when no deleted state is visited. Thus each matrix count is
the required avoidance cardinality, while inclusion--exclusion retains exactly
strings containing every required pattern. Complexity is
`O(2^R * states^3 * log L)` time and `O(states^2)` working memory. Failure
outputs must be propagated before matrices are built; `L=0` is handled by the
identity matrix.

# 31. Two-Faction Networks

## Count coloured graphs, take the logarithm, halve

A **2-coloured graph** assigns each vertex one of two colours and uses only
edges between colours: `b_n = sum_k C(n,k) 2^{k(n-k)}`. Every 2-coloured graph
splits uniquely into connected 2-coloured graphs, so with exponential
generating functions `B = exp(C)`, where `C` counts the connected ones. A
connected bipartite graph has exactly two proper 2-colourings, so the answer
is `n! [x^n] log B / 2`.

All `b_n` at once: `k(n-k) = (n^2 - k^2 - (n-k)^2)/2`. Since
`998244353 = 1 (mod 8)`, `s = sqrt(2)` exists (`s = z + z^{-1}` for a primitive
8th root of unity `z`), and

```text
b_n / n! = s^{n^2} * sum_k ( s^{-k^2} / k! ) ( s^{-(n-k)^2} / (n-k)! ),
```

one self-convolution.

**Correctness.** The exponential formula applies because labelled 2-coloured
graphs are sets of connected 2-coloured components. A connected bipartite
graph's colouring is fixed once one vertex's colour is chosen.

**Complexity and traps.** One convolution plus one logarithm,
`O(N log N)`. Reduce exponents `n^2` modulo `p - 1`. The `n = 1` term is `1`
(two colourings of a single vertex, divided by two).

# 32. Exponential Polynomial Ledger

## A polynomial hides behind the geometric factor

Let `S(k) = sum_{i<k} r^i i^d`. For `r = 1`, `S` is a polynomial of degree
`d+1` in `k`. For `r != 1`, summation by parts shows
`S(k) = r^k G(k) + c` with `deg G <= d` and a constant `c`. Compute
`S(0), ..., S(d+1)` directly; the powers `i^d` come from a linear sieve with
`pow` only at primes. Then `G(i) = (S(i) - c) r^{-i}`, and since the
`(d+1)`-th finite difference of `G` vanishes,

```text
sum_i (-1)^{d+1-i} C(d+1,i) S(i) r^{-i}  =  c (r^{-1} - 1)^{d+1},
```

which determines `c` because `r != 1`. Finally evaluate `G` at `n mod p` by
Lagrange interpolation over the points `0..d`, and multiply by
`r^{n mod (p-1)}`.

**Correctness.** Polynomial identities hold over the field, so evaluating at
`n mod p` is valid. `r^n` depends only on `n mod (p-1)` for `r != 0`. `r = 0`
leaves only the term `i = 0`, with `0^0 = 1`.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(d)` field operations plus `O(d / log d)` modular
powers. The Lagrange formula must allow `n mod p <= d`. Use prefix and suffix
products rather than divisions by `x - i`.

# 33. Branching Family Census

## Newton's method on a functional equation

A record is a root with `s` ordered sub-records and `c_s` styles, so its
generating function satisfies `T = x phi(T)` with `phi(z) = sum c_s z^s`. The
equation `F(T) = T - x phi(T) = 0` has `F'(T) = 1 - x phi'(T)`, which is
invertible as a power series. Newton's iteration
`T <- T - F(T)/F'(T)` doubles the number of correct coefficients. Each round
evaluates `phi(T)` and `phi'(T)` by Horner's rule at the current precision.

**Correctness.** If `T` is correct modulo `x^m`, then
`F(T + e) = F(T) + F'(T) e + O(e^2)` with `e = O(x^m)`, so the update is
correct modulo `x^{2m}`. The start `T = c_0 x` is correct modulo `x^2`.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(D M(N))` over all rounds, where `M` is the cost
of a multiplication. With `c_0 = 0` every count is zero. The sample
`(1, 2, 1)` gives the Catalan numbers, and `(1, 1, 1)` gives Motzkin numbers
shifted by one.

# 34. Coin Bag Census

## The logarithm is a harmonic sum

The bag generating function is `prod_i 1/(1 - x^{w_i})`. Its logarithm is

```text
sum over values w of cnt[w] * sum_{k>=1} x^{w k} / k,
```

which costs `sum_w S/w = O(S log S)` to write down. One power-series
exponential then returns every count up to `S`.

**Correctness.** `log(1/(1 - y)) = sum y^k / k`, and the logarithm turns the
product into a sum. Values above `S` contribute nothing below `x^{S+1}`.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(S log S)` for the harmonic sum plus
`O(S log S)` for the exponential. Coin types are distinct even with equal
values, so count multiplicities and do not deduplicate. With one coin of each
value the counts are the partition numbers.

# 35. Staircase Moments

## Euclid on lattice points

Let `F, G, H` be the sums of `q`, `x q`, and `q^2` with
`q = floor((a x + b) / c)`. If `a >= c` or `b >= c`, write
`a = A c + a'` and `b = B c + b'`. Then `q = A x + B + q'`, and the moments of
`q'` together with closed forms for `sum x^j` give the new values. Otherwise,
count the lattice points under the line by rows instead of columns: with
`m = floor((a n + b) / c)`,

```text
F = n m - F',   G = (m n (n+1) - H' - F') / 2,   H = n m (m+1) - 2G' - 2F' - F,
```

where `(F', G', H')` are the moments for `(c, c - b - 1, a, m - 1)`. The pair
`(a, c)` becomes `(c mod a, a)` exactly as in Euclid's algorithm.

**Correctness.** `sum_x q(x)` counts the pairs `(x, y)` with
`1 <= y <= q(x)`, and `y <= q(x)` iff `x > floor((c y - b - 1) / a)`.
Summing the same set over `y` gives the swapped recursion, and weighting by
`x` or by `2y - 1` gives `G` and `H`.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(log max(a, c))` per query. Reduce `n` modulo
`p` only inside polynomial closed forms. The product `a n + b` needs 128 bits
in C++.

# 36. Binomial Ledger

## Prime powers, then CRT

Factor `m = prod p^e`. Modulo `p^e`, write `n! = p^{v(n)} u(n)`, where `v` is
Legendre's valuation and `u(n)` is coprime to `p`. Grouping the factors of
`n!` by blocks of length `p^e` gives

```text
u(n) = pre[p^e]^{floor(n/p^e)} * pre[n mod p^e] * u(floor(n/p)),
```

with `pre[j]` the product of the integers `<= j` coprime to `p` (modulo `p^e`).
Then `C(n,k) = p^{v(n)-v(k)-v(n-k)} u(n) / (u(k) u(n-k))`, which is `0` once
the valuation reaches `e`. Combine the prime powers by CRT.

**Correctness.** The integers in each full block of length `p^e`, with the
multiples of `p` removed, are a reduced residue system. The removed multiples
of `p` contribute `p^{floor(n/p)} floor(n/p)!`, which is where the recursion
comes from.

**Complexity and traps.** Tables of total size at most `m`, and
`O(sum_p log_p n)` per query. `pre[p^e]` is `+-1` (Wilson's theorem), so its
power costs nothing. When `k > n` the answer is `0`. When `m = 1` every answer
is `0`.

# 37. Rabbit Cycle

## A matrix order with a provable multiple

`F(i + L) = F(i)` for all `i` iff `M^L = I` for `M = [[1,1],[1,0]]` modulo `m`.
By CRT the period is the lcm over the prime powers of `m`. Modulo a prime
`p`, the roots of `x^2 - x - 1` lie in `F_p` when `p = +-1 (mod 5)` (so
`M^{p-1} = I`), are swapped by Frobenius when `p = +-2 (mod 5)` (so
`M^{2(p+1)} = I`), and coincide for `p = 5` (period `20`). Lifting to `p^e`
multiplies the order by at most `p^{e-1}`. Factor this multiple `L` with
Pollard's rho, then divide out each prime while `M^{L/r}` is still the
identity.

**Correctness.** The candidate is a multiple of the true order. Removing
primes while the power stays the identity yields the exact order, since the
order divides every exponent `E` with `M^E = I`. The method needs no
unproved conjecture (such as Wall's).

**Complexity and traps.** Factoring numbers up to `10^18` with Pollard's rho,
plus `O(log^2)` matrix powers per prime. The answer can exceed `m` (up to
`6m`). Matrix products need 128-bit multiplications in C++.

# 38. Exclusive Range Ledger

## Subset XORs form a vector space

The XORs of subsets of `a[l..r]` form a GF(2)-space `V`, and each element of
`V` is produced by exactly `2^{len - dim V}` subsets (a coset of the kernel).
So the answer is `2^{len - rank}` when `x` is in `V`, and `0` otherwise.

Process queries offline by `r`, keeping a basis indexed by leading bit in
which each slot stores the **newest** possible vector. An incoming element
swaps itself into a slot whenever it is newer than the stored vector, and the
older vector continues down. Then the stored vectors with position `>= l`
form an echelon basis of the span of `a[l..r]`.

**Correctness.** By induction on `r`, the vectors with position `>= l` span
exactly the elements of `a[l..r]` and are independent. The swap keeps every
slot as recent as possible, which is the standard exchange argument.

**Complexity and traps.** `O((n + q) B)` with `B = 30`. The empty subset
counts, so `x = 0` always has an answer of at least `1`.

# 39. Divisor Echo Power

## A derivation for Dirichlet convolution

Let `Omega(n)` count prime factors with multiplicity, and set
`D(h)(n) = Omega(n) h(n)`. Because `Omega(xy) = Omega(x) + Omega(y)`,
`D(a # b) = D(a) # b + a # D(b)`. For `g = f^k` this gives
`f # D(g) = k g # D(f)`. Comparing the values at `n`, and using `f(1) = 1`
and `Omega(1) = 0`,

```text
Omega(n) g(n) = sum over d | n, d < n of g(d) f(n/d) (k Omega(n/d) - Omega(d)).
```

Push each finished `g(d)` to its multiples.

**Correctness.** The recurrence determines `g(n)` from smaller divisors
because `Omega(n) >= 1` is invertible modulo the prime. The coefficients of
`f^k` are polynomials in `k`, so `k` may be reduced modulo the prime. For
`k = -1` the result is the Dirichlet inverse.

**Complexity and traps.** Harmonic `O(N log N)`. With `f = 1`, `k = 2` gives
the divisor count and `k = -1` gives the Möbius function.

# 40. Root Census Modulo p

## The distinct roots are a gcd

Over `F_p`, `x^p - x = prod over a of (x - a)`. So `gcd(f, x^p - x)` is the
product of `(x - a)` over the distinct roots of `f`, and its degree is the
answer. Compute `x^p mod f` by square-and-multiply. Each reduction modulo `f`
uses the precomputed series inverse of `f` reversed (Barrett for
polynomials), so a step costs a few polynomial products. Finish with
Euclid's algorithm.

**Correctness.** The roots of `x^p - x` are exactly all elements of `F_p`, each
simple, so the gcd keeps each root of `f` once. The zero polynomial is the
special case in which every residue is a root.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(d^2 log p)` with schoolbook products (C++
accumulates 128-bit sums lazily), or Kronecker substitution in Python.
Normalize the coefficients modulo `p` first; the leading coefficient may
vanish.

# 41. Sprinkler Coverage Area

## Green's theorem on the uncovered arcs

The area of the union equals half the boundary integral of `x dy - y dx`. The
boundary consists of the arcs of each circle not covered by the other discs.
Remove duplicates and discs contained in others. For circle `i`, every
overlapping circle `j` covers one angular interval centred at the direction
of `j`, with half-width `acos((r_i^2 + d^2 - r_j^2) / (2 r_i d))`. Sweep the
sorted intervals and integrate each uncovered arc in closed form.

**Correctness.** After the removals, every boundary point of the union lies
on exactly one circle's uncovered arcs (tangencies have measure zero), and
the arcs are oriented counterclockwise.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(n^2 log n)`. Identical circles must be merged,
or both would be considered covered. Externally tangent circles must not
produce intervals.

# 42. Crystal Hull Surface

## Incremental hull with a horizon

Start from a non-degenerate tetrahedron, with faces stored counterclockwise
from outside. For each further point, find the faces it sees (strictly
positive orientation). Delete them, and connect every horizon edge (a visible
face adjacent to an invisible one) to the point, keeping the edge's
orientation. Points that see no face are inside and are skipped. The answer
is the sum of the triangle areas.

**Correctness.** The visible faces form a connected cap. Replacing it by the
cone from the new point over its boundary yields the hull of the old hull
plus the point. The statement's guarantee (no supporting plane contains four
points) makes every face a triangle and every orientation test decisive.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(n F) = O(n^2)` face tests. Orientations of
coordinates up to `10^9` need 128 bits. The initial tetrahedron needs four
affinely independent points.

# 43. Triangle Census Queries

## Points below segments

For `x_i < x_j`, let `below(i, j)` be the number of points strictly between
them in `x` and strictly below segment `ij`. Around each `i`, sort the points
to its right by slope. Point `k` is below `ij` iff its slope from `i` is
smaller and `x_k < x_j`, a dominance count kept with a Fenwick tree or sorted
insertion. For a triangle with vertices sorted by `x` as `a, b, c`, the
answer is `below(a,b) + below(b,c) - below(a,c)` when `b` is above `ac`, and
`below(a,c) - below(a,b) - below(b,c) - 1` otherwise.

**Correctness.** The region under the path `a, b, c` minus the region under
`ac` is the triangle when `b` is above. In the other case the roles swap and
`b` itself is counted once under `ac`. Distinct `x` coordinates and no three
collinear points leave no boundary cases.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(n^2 log n)` preprocessing, `O(1)` per query, and
`O(n^2)` memory. Compare slopes with exact cross products.

# 44. Polygon Triangulation Count

## Interval DP over internal diagonals

Exactly one triangle of every triangulation sits on the edge `(0, n-1)`. Its
apex `k` splits the polygon into the chains `0..k` and `k..n-1`, each closed
by an internal diagonal. So
`T[i][j] = sum_k T[i][k] T[k][j]` over valid chords `(i,k)` and `(k,j)`.
A chord is an internal diagonal iff it lies in the interior angle at both
endpoints (cone test) and properly crosses no edge.

**Correctness.** In a triangulation the triangles adjacent to a chord split
the chord's region into two independent sub-polygons, and the decomposition
by the apex is unique.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(n^3)` for both validity and the DP. Normalize
to counterclockwise order. Reflex vertices need the complemented cone test.

# 45. Obstacle Shortcut

## Shortest paths bend only at corners

A shortest path avoiding open convex obstacles is a polyline whose interior
vertices are obstacle corners: anywhere else it could be shortened locally.
Build the visibility graph on `S`, `T`, and all corners, then run Dijkstra.
Segment `PQ` is blocked iff some point of it is strictly inside an obstacle.
Intersect `t in [0,1]` with the open half-planes of the obstacle's edges, and
compare the resulting bounds as exact fractions.

**Correctness.** Touching walls and corners is allowed, so only strict
interior points block. The clipping interval is exactly the set of
parameters whose points are strictly inside.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(V^2 E)` for visibility and `O(V^2 log V)` for
Dijkstra. Segments between two corners of the same building are edges
(allowed) or diagonals (blocked). Use 128-bit integers for the fractions.

# 46. Lantern Grid

## Light chasing

Presses commute and are linear over GF(2). Treat the first row's presses as
unknowns. Lamp `(r, c)` can then only be turned off by the press below it,
which determines row `r+1` as an affine function of the unknowns (a bitset of
`m` coefficients plus a constant). The last row of lamps gives `m` equations.
If they are consistent, the answer is `2^{m - rank}`, and otherwise `0`.
Transpose so that `m <= n`.

**Correctness.** Every press set satisfying the first `n-1` lamp rows is
determined by its first row, and the remaining equations are exactly the
last-row lamps.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(n m^2 / w)` with word size `w`. Known values:
the empty 4×4 board has 16 solutions, and the 19×19 board has nullity 16.

# 47. Quorum Circle

## Binary search, pin a point to the boundary

Feasibility is monotone in `R`. An optimal disc can be translated until one
of its points, `p`, lies on the boundary. The centre then lies on the circle
of radius `R` around `p`, and every other point `q` with `|pq| <= 2R`
restricts the centre to an arc of half-width `acos(|pq| / 2R)` around the
direction of `q`. The deepest overlap of these arcs, plus coincident points,
decides feasibility.

**Correctness.** Translating a disc while it keeps its points never loses
any, until a point reaches the boundary. Each arc is exactly the set of
centres at distance at most `R` from `q`.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(n^2 log n)` per probe, and about 60 probes.
Coincident points belong to every candidate disc. `k = 1` gives `0`.

# 48. Quiet Committee Census

## Meet in the middle

Split the members into halves `A` and `B`. For every subset `M` of `B`,
compute `best[M]` and `ways[M]` (the optimum and the number of optimal
committees inside `M`) by branching on the lowest member `v`: either `v` is
out (`M - v`), or `v` is in (`M - N[v]`, plus `w[v]`). Then enumerate the
committees `S` inside `A`. Each leaves exactly `B - N(S)` available, so
combine with `best` and `ways` of that set.

**Correctness.** Every committee splits uniquely into its `A` part and its
`B` part. The `B` part ranges over exactly the committees inside `B - N(S)`.
The branching on `v` is a partition, so counts add.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(2^{n/2})` time and memory. With zero weights
every committee ties, so the count is the number of independent sets (for
example `2^40` on the empty graph). Repeated rivalries are harmless.

# 49. Glacier Cut

## Binary searches on a convex polygon

Let `f(p) = cross(B - A, p - A)` (positive means left of the line). Edge
directions of a counterclockwise convex polygon increase in angle, so the
vertex maximizing `f` is the start of the first edge whose angle is at least
the direction of the line. The minimizing vertex is found symmetrically.
Between them `f` is monotone along both chains, and binary searches find the
two edges where it changes sign. The left piece is a range of vertices plus
the two crossing points, so its area is a prefix shoelace sum plus three
correction terms. Computing the crossing points as exact rationals keeps
even tiny slivers accurate.

**Correctness.** Unimodality of a linear function on a convex polygon makes
all searches valid. The piece left of the line is exactly the convex polygon
formed by the crossing points and the vertices with `f > 0`.

**Complexity and traps.** `O(log n)` per query. Lines that miss the polygon
or only touch it give `0` or the full area. The numerators reach about
`10^33`, so C++ uses 128-bit integers.

# 50. Chronicle Path Dictionary

## Turn path occurrences into root-path suffix tests

Let `w = LCA(u,v)`. Split `S(u,v)` into the upward part `A` (from `u` up to
`w`, inclusive) and the downward part `B` (below `w`, down to `v`). Every
occurrence lies inside `A`, inside `B`, or crosses the junction between them.

Read upward from its lowest vertex `x`, an occurrence inside `A` spells `p`.
Equivalently, the root-to-`x` string **ends with** `reverse(p)`. An
occurrence inside `B` that ends at vertex `y` means the root-to-`y` string
ends with `p`. So both kinds of occurrence become "ends with" tests on
root-to-vertex strings.

Build one Aho--Corasick automaton for all patterns and their reversals, and
run it down the tree: the state of `x` is the automaton state reached on the
root-to-`x` string. A string ends with a dictionary word `t` exactly when its
state lies in the fail-tree subtree of `t`'s node, which is an interval of the
fail-tree Euler order.

Occurrences inside `A` are the vertices `x` on the vertical segment from `u`
up to depth `depth(w)+|p|-1` whose state lies in that interval. That count is
(count on the root path of `u`) minus (count on the root path of the segment
top's parent). One DFS maintains a Fenwick tree over the Euler positions of
the states on the current root path and evaluates every such event. `B` is
symmetric, with bottom vertex `v` and top depth `depth(w)+|p|`.

A crossing occurrence uses at most `|p|-1` vertices on each side of the
junction. Extract those at most `2|p|-2` letters (one ancestor jump plus a
walk) and run KMP, counting only matches that start before the junction and
end after it.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** For a vertex `x` and a word `t`, the root-to-`x` string ends with
`t` iff the automaton state of `x` is in the fail-subtree of node(`t`).

*Proof.* The automaton state is the longest suffix of the read text that is a
trie prefix. Its fail chain lists every suffix of the text that is a trie
prefix, longest first. `t` is such a suffix iff node(`t`) is on that chain,
i.e. iff node(`t`) is an ancestor of the state in the fail tree.

**Lemma 2.** The three counted families partition all occurrences, and each
family is counted exactly.

*Proof.* An occurrence occupies consecutive positions of `A+B`. It lies before
the junction, after it, or covers both sides of it. An occurrence inside `A`
has a unique lowest vertex, on the stated segment, and it satisfies Lemma 1
with `reverse(p)`. Conversely, such a vertex yields an occurrence that stays
inside `A` by the depth bound. The case of `B` is symmetric. Crossing
occurrences are exactly the matches of the extracted window that start before
the junction and end after it.

**Theorem.** The printed value is the number of occurrences of `p` in
`S(u,v)`.

*Proof.* The Fenwick tree holds exactly the states of the current root path,
so each event returns the count of Lemma 1 on that root path. Differences of
root paths give vertical segments. Lemma 2 completes the sum.

## Complexity and traps

The automaton has at most `2S+1` states for total pattern length `S`. Building
it, the Euler tour, and the DFS take `O((n + S) log S)` with the Fenwick tree,
and each query adds `O(log n + |p|)`. Letters on the upward side must be read
toward the root. `S(v,u)` is the reverse of `S(u,v)`. The crossing window
must include `w` itself on the `A` side. Recursion depth reaches `n`, so every
DFS is iterative.

# 51. Echo Census

## From squares to runs

A **run** is a maximal substring `s[a..b)` with smallest period `p` and
length at least `2p`. Write an echo as `ww` with `w = u^k`, where `u` is
primitive. Then `ww` has smallest period `|u|` and length at least `2|u|`, so
it lies inside a unique run of period `|u|`, with half-length `k|u|`.

Inside one run of period `p`, the echoes of half-length `L = kp` start at
`a, a+1, ..., b-2L`, and the echoes starting at `x` and `x+p` are equal. Hence
the first `min(p, b-2L-a+1)` starting points already give every such echo of
that run. Enumerate those for every run and multiple `L`, and deduplicate by
`(hash, length)`.

The runs themselves come from the runs theorem. Fix one of the two letter
orders; the end of the string is smaller than every letter in both. Let
`lyn[i]` be the length of the longest Lyndon word starting at `i`. Every run
of period `p` contains, for one of the two orders, a position `i` with
`lyn[i] = p`. Extending that root left and right with longest-common-extension
queries recovers the whole run. The Lyndon array follows from the
next-smaller-suffix recurrence `j += lyn[j]`, whose suffix comparisons are
LCE queries.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** Every echo lies in some run whose period is the length of its
primitive root.

*Proof.* `ww` with `w = u^k` has period `|u|` and length `2k|u| >= 2|u|`, and
`|u|` is its smallest period by Fine and Wilf. Extending it maximally while
keeping that period gives a run containing it.

**Lemma 2.** In a run of period `p`, the echo of half-length `L` starting at
`x` equals the one starting at `x+p`, whenever both lie in the run.

*Proof.* Both substrings have length `2L` and lie in a string of period `p`.
Shifting by the period does not change the letters.

**Lemma 3.** The Lyndon-root procedure outputs exactly the runs.

*Proof.* This is the runs theorem: each run has an L-root for one of the two
orders, and the longest Lyndon word starting there is exactly that root.
Conversely, every reported interval has period `p` and is maximal because both
extensions stop at a mismatch or at an end of the string.

**Theorem.** The program prints the number of distinct echoes.

*Proof.* By Lemmas 1 and 3 every echo is some `ww` enumerated from its run. By
Lemma 2 the restricted starting points lose none. Deduplication counts each
string once.

## Complexity and traps

The number of runs is below `n`, and the enumerated `(start, L)` pairs are
bounded by the sum over runs of `min(p, len - 2L + 1)` over multiples `L`,
which stays `O(n log n)`. Each LCE costs `O(log n)` by galloping plus binary
search on prefix hashes, giving `O(n log n)` overall. Trap: in the Lyndon
recurrence, a suffix that is a prefix of the other suffix is the **smaller**
one in both orders, so the comparison must be handled before comparing
letters.

# 52. Tariff Revision Network

## Divide and conquer over the revision timeline

Recursively solve a time interval `[l,r]` of revisions. Links revised inside
the interval are *dynamic*; every other link has a fixed tariff there.

1. **Contraction.** Union all dynamic links first, then run Kruskal on the
   static links. A static link still accepted is in *every* minimum spanning
   tree of every moment in `[l,r]`. Add its tariff to a running total and
   contract its endpoints.
2. **Reduction.** On the contracted graph, run Kruskal on the static links
   alone. A static link rejected now closes a cycle of cheaper static links
   and is never needed in `[l,r]`, so drop it.

After both steps an interval with `k` dynamic links keeps `O(k)` vertices and
static edges. Split the interval, and at a single revision apply it and run
Kruskal on the tiny remaining graph.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** A static link chosen during contraction belongs to some MST at
every moment of `[l,r]`.

*Proof.* Whatever tariffs the dynamic links take, it is at most as good as
treating them as infinitely cheap. Kruskal with the dynamic links first
accepts the static link `e` only if its endpoints are not yet connected by
dynamic links plus cheaper static links. By the cut property, `e` is then a
minimum edge across some cut for every assignment of dynamic tariffs.

**Lemma 2.** A static link rejected during reduction belongs to no needed MST
at any moment of `[l,r]`.

*Proof.* It closes a cycle of static links that are no more expensive and
whose tariffs are fixed in the interval. By the cycle property it can be
replaced in every spanning tree.

**Theorem.** Each printed value is the MST weight after that revision.

*Proof.* By Lemmas 1 and 2 each recursion level preserves the MST weight of
every moment of its interval (plus the accumulated contracted weight). A leaf
computes it directly.

## Complexity and traps

Every level processes `O(q)` edges in total, so the time is
`O((m + q) log q log m)` with sorting and the memory is `O(m + q log q)`.
Revisions must be applied in time order: the left half runs before the right
half reads the updated tariffs. Self-loops and parallel links are handled by
the DSU. Stamp dynamic links with a fresh counter per call, not with `l`.

# 53. Spanning Weight Spectrum

## Weights as exponents

Give a cable of weight `w` the formal weight `x^w` in the Laplacian. By the
matrix-tree theorem any cofactor equals

```text
F(x) = sum over spanning trees T of x^(weight(T)),
```

so the coefficient of `x^W` is the requested count. `F` has degree at most
`D = (n-1)K`. Evaluate `F(0), ..., F(D)` by modular Gaussian elimination and
interpolate the coefficients in `O(D^2)` with the master polynomial
`prod(x - i)` and synthetic division.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** For a numeric `x`, the determinant of the reduced Laplacian with
entries built from `x^w` equals `F(x)`.

*Proof.* The weighted matrix-tree theorem states that the cofactor equals the
sum over spanning trees of the product of edge weights, here
`x^(sum of w)`. Self-loops contribute nothing to a Laplacian.

**Lemma 2.** `D+1` distinct evaluation points determine a polynomial of
degree at most `D` over the field `Z/998244353`.

*Proof.* The Vandermonde matrix of distinct points is invertible; Lagrange's
formula writes the unique interpolant.

**Theorem.** The output lists the number of spanning trees of each weight
modulo the prime.

*Proof.* Lemma 1 gives correct values of `F` modulo the prime, and Lemma 2
recovers its coefficients.

## Complexity and traps

`O(D n^3 + D^2)` time, which is at most about `9.5 * 10^7` field operations at
the limits, and `O(n^2 + D)` memory. `0^0 = 1` makes weight-0 cables count at
`x = 0`. A disconnected graph gives the zero polynomial, and `n = 1` prints
the single empty tree.

# 54. Fleet Pairing

## Primal--dual blossom algorithm

Maximum-weight matching in a general graph is solved by Edmonds' blossom
algorithm with dual variables. Every vertex carries `y_v` (initially the
maximum weight) and every odd set `B` carries `z_B >= 0`. We keep all edges
feasible, `y_u + y_v + sum z_B >= 2w(uv)`, and grow alternating trees from all
free vertices using only *tight* edges. An edge between two outer vertices of
different trees augments; one inside a tree closes an odd cycle, which is
shrunk to a blossom. When no tight edge helps, change the duals by the
smallest of four bounds:

1. an outer vertex dual reaches zero;
2. an edge from an outer vertex to a free vertex becomes tight;
3. an edge between two outer blossoms becomes tight;
4. an inner blossom's `z` reaches zero, which expands it.

Parallel offers keep only the best one. Weights are doubled so that every
dual change stays an integer.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** Throughout the algorithm the duals are feasible and every matched
edge and every blossom's internal matched structure stay tight.

*Proof.* The delta choice is the minimum of exactly the quantities that would
first violate feasibility or nonnegativity. Tree vertices move in opposite
directions along every tight tree edge.

**Lemma 2.** At termination the complementary-slackness conditions hold:
matched edges are tight, positive-`z` blossoms are full, and every free vertex
has `y_v = 0`.

*Proof.* A stage ends either by augmentation or by delta type 1, which drives
the duals of all outer vertices, in particular all free vertices, to zero.
Blossoms with positive `z` are only created as tight odd cycles, and
augmentation preserves their near-perfect matchings.

**Theorem.** The final matching has maximum weight.

*Proof.* By Edmonds' LP description of the matching polytope, feasible duals
bound every matching's weight from above. Lemma 2 gives equality for the
constructed matching.

## Complexity and traps

There are `O(n)` stages with `O(n)` dual changes each, and each change costs
`O(n)` thanks to the per-blossom best-edge lists. That is `O(n^3)` time and
`O(n + m)` memory. Handling blossoms inside blossoms is where implementations
go wrong: relabel with the stored endpoint lists, rotate children on
augmentation, and expand zero-dual blossoms at the end of a stage.

# 55. Monsoon Diameter

## Paths as points

A path with totals `(A, B) = (sum a, sum b)` takes `A t + B` on day `t`. The
answer on day `t` is the maximum of these linear functions: the upper
envelope of the point set restricted to `t >= 0`. There are `O(n^2)` paths,
but only `O(n log n)` candidate points are needed.

Split every vertex of degree above three with zero-cost dummy vertices; path
totals do not change. Now choose an edge that splits the component into two
parts of sizes at least about a third each. The paths through that edge are
sums of one root-to-vertex vector from each side plus the edge itself. The
useful ones lie on the Minkowski sum of the two sides' upper hulls, which has
linear size and is computed by merging slopes. Recurse on both sides. Finally
take the hull of all candidates and sweep `t` upward with a pointer.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** For vectors `P` and `Q` and every `t >= 0`,
`max over p+q in P+Q of f_t(p+q) = max_P f_t + max_Q f_t`, where
`f_t(A,B) = At+B`. So only hull points of each side matter, and hull(P+Q) is
the Minkowski sum of the hulls.

*Proof.* The function `f_t` is linear, and a linear maximum over a sum set
separates into the two maxima. The vertices of the Minkowski sum of two convex
polygons are sums of vertices, merged by edge slope.

**Lemma 2.** Every path is represented at the unique decomposition edge where
its two endpoints are first separated, or it has zero length.

*Proof.* Recursion removes edges. The first removed edge on the path splits
it into two root-to-vertex pieces inside that component.

**Theorem.** The printed sequence is the maximum path length on each day.

*Proof.* By Lemma 2 every path's value is dominated by some candidate, and by
Lemma 1 no maximum is lost in the hulls. The final sweep evaluates the
envelope correctly because its optimal point moves monotonically to larger `A`
as `t` grows.

## Complexity and traps

Degree at most three makes the edge-centroid split balanced, so the depth is
`O(log n)` and the total work is `O(n log^2 n + m)`. Coordinates reach
`10^16`, so cross products need 128 bits in C++. Keep the point `(0,0)` for a
single-village path, and drop the hull part before the maximum-`B` point,
because it never wins for `t >= 0`.

# 56. Window Substring Census

## Count each substring at its last occurrence

Sweep `r` from left to right. For each distinct substring `t` of `s[1..r]`,
look at its last occurrence ending at or before `r`. That occurrence starts
at `>= l` exactly when `t` occurs in `s[l..r]`. So give `+1` to the start
position of every such last occurrence; the answer to `(l, r)` is then the
sum over starts in `[l, r]`.

In the suffix automaton of `s`, the suffixes of `s[1..r]` are the states on
the suffix-link path from the prefix state `P_r` to the root. The substrings
of one state share their end positions, so they also share their last end
`e <= r`. A state with lengths `(len(link), len]` contributes the starts
`[e-len+1, e-len(link)]`.

Keep the suffix-link tree in a link--cut tree in which every preferred path
has one colour, its common `e`. Moving from `r-1` to `r`, `access(P_r)`
recolours the root path of `P_r` to `r`. Each preferred-path chain
`top..x` that it absorbs contributes a contiguous length block, so its old
starts are removed with one range update. The whole path then contributes the
starts `[1, r]`.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** After processing `r`, the colour of a state is the largest end
position `<= r` of its substrings, or `0` if none has occurred yet.

*Proof.* A state's substrings end at `r` iff the state is on the root path of
`P_r`. Access recolours exactly that path with `r`.

**Lemma 2.** The range-add structure holds, for every start position, the
number of distinct substrings whose last occurrence (ending at or before `r`)
starts there.

*Proof.* By Lemma 1 the contribution of every state is determined by its
colour. Access removes each changed chain's old block and adds the new one.
Chains in one splay tree cover contiguous length ranges because lengths
increase strictly along the root path.

**Theorem.** For every window the output is the number of distinct substrings
of `s[l..r]`.

*Proof.* A substring occurs in `s[l..r]` iff its last occurrence ending at or
before `r` starts at or after `l`, and by Lemma 2 the range sum over `[l, r]`
counts exactly those.

## Complexity and traps

Access performs `O(log n)` amortized preferred-child changes, each with a
Fenwick update, so the time is `O(n log^2 n + q log n)` and the memory is
`O(n sigma)`. The root state has length `0` and contributes nothing. Use the
leftmost node of the splayed subtree as the chain top, and push the colour
tags before reading them.

# 57. Prime Power Xor Sum

## Min_25 sieve

`f` is multiplicative with `f(p) = p xor 1`, which is `p - 1` for odd `p` and
`3` for `p = 2`. The only values that matter are the `O(sqrt N)` distinct
quotients `v = floor(N / i)`.

1. **Lucy DP.** For each such `v`, compute the number and the sum of primes up
   to `v` by sieving out, for each prime `p <= sqrt N`, the numbers whose least
   prime factor is `p`:
   `g(v) -= p^j (g(v/p) - g(p-1))`.
2. **Composite part.** Let `S(v, j)` be the sum of `f(i)` over `2 <= i <= v`
   whose least prime factor exceeds `p_j`. Then

   ```text
   S(v,j) = F_prime(v) - F_prime(p_j)
          + sum_{k>j, p_k^2<=v} sum_{e>=1, p_k^(e+1)<=v}
              ( f(p_k^e) S(v/p_k^e, k) + f(p_k^(e+1)) ).
   ```

The answer is `S(N, 0) + 1`.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** After processing all primes `<= sqrt v`, `g(v)` counts (or sums)
exactly the primes up to `v`.

*Proof.* Processing `p` removes the numbers in `[2, v]` whose least prime
factor is `p`. They are `p` times the numbers `m` with least prime factor at
least `p`, i.e. the terms of `g(v/p) - g(p-1)`. Composite numbers up to `v`
have least prime factor `<= sqrt v`.

**Lemma 2.** The recurrence for `S` counts every `i` with least prime factor
`> p_j` exactly once.

*Proof.* A prime `i` is counted in the prime term. A composite `i` factors
uniquely as `p_k^e * m` with `p_k` its least prime factor and `m` having least
prime factor `> p_k`. Either `m > 1`, counted in `S(v/p_k^e, k)`, or `m = 1`
and `e >= 2`, counted by the `f(p_k^(e+1))` terms. Multiplicativity gives
`f(i) = f(p_k^e) f(m)`.

**Theorem.** The output equals `sum_{i<=N} f(i)` modulo the prime.

*Proof.* By Lemmas 1 and 2, plus `f(1) = 1`.

## Complexity and traps

`O(N^{3/4} / log N)` time and `O(sqrt N)` memory. `f(2) = 3` differs from
`p - 1`, so correct it in the prime sums. Values of `f` can be `0` (for
example `f(4) = 2 xor 2`), so never divide by `f`. Compute the square root
exactly.

# 58. Critical Link Audit

## Dominators after subdividing links

Replace every link `u -> v` by `u -> x_e -> v` with a new vertex `x_e`. Closing
link `e` equals deleting `x_e`. A station becomes unreachable exactly when
every path to it from `1` passes through `x_e`, i.e. when `x_e` dominates it.
So the answer for `e` is the number of original stations in the subtree of
`x_e` in the dominator tree. Compute the tree with Lengauer--Tarjan
(semi-dominators, path-compressed link--eval) on `n + m` vertices.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** A reachable station `t` is disconnected by closing `e` iff `x_e`
dominates `t` in the subdivided graph.

*Proof.* Paths in the original graph avoiding `e` correspond to paths in the
subdivided graph avoiding `x_e`, and conversely.

**Lemma 2.** The dominators of `t` are exactly its ancestors in the dominator
tree.

*Proof.* This is the defining property of the tree built from immediate
dominators, and Lengauer--Tarjan computes those immediate dominators
correctly.

**Theorem.** Each output is the number of stations lost when that link closes.

*Proof.* By Lemmas 1 and 2 the lost stations are the original vertices in the
subtree of `x_e`. An unreachable `x_e` loses nothing.

## Complexity and traps

`O((n + m) log(n + m))` with simple path compression, and linear memory. The
DFS and `eval` must be iterative. Parallel links correctly lose nothing
because their subdivision vertices do not dominate each other. Unreachable
links print `0`.

# 59. Walk Count Oracle

## A recurrence hidden in the matrix

Let `a_i = e_s^T A^i e_t` be the number of journeys of length `i`. By the
Cayley--Hamilton theorem, the characteristic polynomial of `A` annihilates
`A`, so `(a_i)` satisfies a linear recurrence of order at most `n`. Compute
`a_0, ..., a_{2n+1}` by `2n + 2` sparse vector steps. Berlekamp--Massey then
returns the shortest recurrence `Q` consistent with them, which is the true
minimal recurrence. Finally `[x^N] P(x)/Q(x)` with `P = (a Q) mod x^L` comes
from Bostan--Mori: replace `P/Q` by `P(x)Q(-x) / Q(x)Q(-x)` and keep the
even or odd part, halving `N` each round.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** The sequence has a linear recurrence of order at most `n`, valid
from index `0`, possibly with a nilpotent transient.

*Proof.* Take the minimal polynomial `mu` of `A`, of degree `<= n`. Then
`e_s^T A^i mu(A) e_t = 0` for all `i`, which is exactly such a recurrence.

**Lemma 2.** Given `2L` terms of a sequence with a recurrence of order at most
`L`, Berlekamp--Massey outputs a recurrence valid for the whole sequence.

*Proof.* Two recurrences of orders `L1, L2` that agree on `L1 + L2` terms
generate the same sequence. The algorithm returns the shortest recurrence for
the prefix, whose order is at most `L`.

**Theorem.** The output is `a_N` modulo the prime.

*Proof.* By Lemmas 1 and 2, `A(x) = P(x)/Q(x)` as formal series. Each
Bostan--Mori step preserves the coefficient `[x^N]` of `P/Q`.

## Complexity and traps

`O(n m + n^2 log N)` with schoolbook products (`O(n log n log N)` with
FFT-based products). Powering the `n x n` matrix directly, at `n^3 log N`, is
far too slow. Keep the transient: build `P` from the actual first `L` terms
instead of assuming a pure recurrence. `N = 0` counts the empty journey when
`s = t`.

# 60. Taxicab Backbone

## Bottlenecks live on a Manhattan MST

The minimum possible largest hop between two beacons equals the largest edge
on their path in any minimum spanning tree of the complete Manhattan graph
(the minimax path property of MSTs). Some MST uses only candidate edges from
each point to its nearest neighbour in each of the eight 45-degree octants. A
sweep in decreasing `x` with a Fenwick tree over `y - x`, minimizing `x + y`,
finds one octant's nearest neighbours, and four coordinate transforms cover
all eight octants. Answer queries during Kruskal: each component keeps its
pending queries, merging moves the smaller list, and a query whose endpoints
join is answered by the current edge weight.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** For each point and each octant, the nearest point in that octant
is enough: some MST uses only these edges.

*Proof.* If `q` and `r` are both in point `p`'s octant and `q` is the nearest,
then `|q - r| <= |p - r|` in Manhattan distance. So edge `pr` is a maximum on
the cycle `p, q, r` and can be discarded by the cycle property.

**Lemma 2.** Kruskal answers a query `(s, t)` with the weight of the edge that
first joins their components, which is the minimax bottleneck.

*Proof.* Components after all edges of weight `< w` are exactly the classes of
routes with maximum hop `< w`.

**Theorem.** Every printed value is the minimum required strength.

*Proof.* Combine Lemmas 1 and 2. Small-to-large moving keeps every pending
query in the list of one of its endpoints' components.

## Complexity and traps

`O(n log n + q log q)` time. The sweep's ties decide which of two equal points
sees the other, so sort by `(x, y)` and query before inserting. Distances
reach `4 * 10^9`, beyond 32 bits. `s = t` answers `0`.

# 61. Cavern Descent

## Lines from descendants

`dp[v] = min over proper descendants u of a[v] * b[u] + dp[u]`, and exits have
`dp = 0`. The descendant `u` is the line `y = b[u] X + dp[u]`, queried at
`X = a[v]`. Each vertex needs a structure holding its subtree's lines that
supports minimum queries at a point and merging with its children's
structures. Li Chao trees over `X in [-10^5, 10^5]` merge by re-inserting the
line of each node of the smaller tree into the other while walking both trees
in parallel.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** A Li Chao tree query returns the minimum over all inserted lines
at `X`.

*Proof.* Each node keeps the line that is better at its midpoint. The loser
can only win on one side, where it is inserted. The query visits every node
whose interval contains `X`.

**Lemma 2.** Merging tree `B` into tree `A` yields a Li Chao tree over the
union of their lines.

*Proof.* Each line of `B` is inserted into `A` at the position of its node or
above it. Insertion is valid from any node whose interval contains the line's
useful region, and the recursion processes every node of `B`.

**Theorem.** `dp` is computed correctly for every chamber.

*Proof.* Process vertices in post-order. Before `v` is queried, its structure
contains exactly the lines of its proper descendants (Lemma 2). Lemma 1 gives
the minimum.

## Complexity and traps

A line only moves downward during merges, so the total merge work is
`O(n log C)` with `C = 2 * 10^5 + 1`, plus `O(n log C)` for queries. Recycle
the emptied nodes of merged trees to keep the memory linear. `dp` values reach
`2 * 10^15`, so use 64 bits. The root is not an exit unless `n = 1`.

# 62. Window Component Census

## Keep the newest spanning forest

Scan cables `1, 2, ..., m` while maintaining a spanning forest that prefers
newer cables. When cable `i` joins two vertices that are already connected,
remove the oldest cable on the path between them and insert `i`. Record the
removed index as `pre[i]`: `0` when nothing is removed, and `i` for a
self-loop. The forest lives in a link--cut tree whose cable nodes carry their
index as weight, with path-minimum aggregates.

A window `[l, r]` has `n - #{i in [l, r] : pre[i] < l}` components, counted
offline by sorting queries by `l` and cables by `pre`.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** After processing cable `r`, for every `l <= r` the forest cables
with index `>= l` form a spanning forest of the graph on cables `l..r`.

*Proof.* The forest is a maximum spanning forest with respect to cable index,
and the cut and cycle properties hold for that order. Restricting a maximum
spanning forest to weights `>= l` gives a spanning forest of the subgraph with
those weights.

**Lemma 2.** Cable `i <= r` is in the forest after step `r` with index `>= l`,
and contributes to that spanning forest, iff `pre[i] < l`.

*Proof.* Cable `i` joins two components of the graph on cables `pre[i]+1..i`
but not of the graph on cables `pre[i]..i`. Hence it merges components within
`[l, i]` iff `l > pre[i]`, and cables merging components are exactly the
forest edges of Lemma 1.

**Theorem.** Each answer equals the number of components of the window's graph.

*Proof.* Components equal `n` minus the forest size. By Lemma 2 the forest
size is the counted quantity.

## Complexity and traps

`O((m + q) log n)` amortized with the link--cut tree and a Fenwick tree, and
`O(n + m + q)` memory. Cable nodes separate parallel cables so that the
oldest one can be cut. Self-loops never merge components. Cut both halves of
the replaced cable node.

# 63. Periodic Loop Frontier

## Plug DP produces a recurrence

Process the floor row by row and cell by cell with a broken-profile DP. A
state stores `W + 1` plugs, each empty, an opening bracket, or a closing
bracket. Matching brackets are the two ends of one path fragment. Every cell
must have degree two. Joining two opening (or two closing) brackets
re-matches the partner, and joining a matched pair would close a loop, which
is allowed only at the last cell of a row when no other plug is open. That
closing transition contributes `a_N`, the count for `N` rows.

Row-boundary profiles form a finite set `U`, and
`a_N = c^T T^(N-1) v` for the row transfer matrix `T`. Thus `(a_N)` has a
linear recurrence of order at most `|U|` (`1117` for `W = 10`). Generate
`2|U| + 8` terms, recover the recurrence with Berlekamp--Massey, and jump to
`N` with Bostan--Mori.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** The DP counts sets of moves in which every processed cell has
degree two and the moves form one cycle.

*Proof.* Brackets encode the non-crossing pairing of path ends on the
frontier. Each transition preserves that encoding. Forbidding a pair to close
early prevents extra cycles, and requiring an empty profile at closing forces
all cells to be covered by that single cycle.

**Lemma 2.** Once the cumulative set of reachable row profiles stops growing
for one row, it is closed under the row transition.

*Proof.* The successors of the new row's profiles are successors of profiles
already seen, which were already recorded.

**Theorem.** The output is the number of patrols modulo the prime.

*Proof.* By Lemma 1 the generated terms are correct. Lemma 2 bounds the
recurrence order by the recorded `|U|`, so `2|U|` terms determine it (as in
Problem 59).

## Complexity and traps

With `S` the number of mid-row states, the plug DP costs `O(|U| W S)`,
Berlekamp--Massey costs `O(|U|^2)`, and Bostan--Mori costs
`O(|U|^2 log N)`. Directly powering the `1117 x 1117` transfer matrix would
need about `10^11` operations. The DP matches the known counts (`37` for
`4 x 6`, `4638576` for `8 x 8`) and `a(W,N) = a(N,W)`.

# 64. Beacon Placement

## Binary search plus 2-SAT

Binary search the answer `d`: is there a placement with all pairwise
distances `>= d`? Sort the `2n` sites. Literal `k` says "the owner of site
`k` uses site `k`"; its negation is the owner's other site. Choosing site `k`
forbids every other site strictly closer than `d`, which is a contiguous block
of the sorted order. Build a segment tree whose leaf for site `j` implies
"the owner of `j` uses its other site". Then `k` implies `O(log n)` tree
nodes, and 2-SAT (Tarjan's SCC) decides the question.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** A placement with minimum distance `>= d` is exactly an assignment
satisfying, for every pair of chosen sites `j != k` with distance `< d`, the
clause `not(k) or not(j)`.

*Proof.* The clause forbids choosing both sites of a close pair. Each beacon
picks exactly one of its two literals by the pairing of negations.

**Lemma 2.** The segment-tree graph has a path from `k` to `not(j)` iff `j` is
within distance `< d` of `k` and `j != k`.

*Proof.* Tree edges only go downward, from a covering node to its leaves, and
each leaf leads to the negation of its site. The range of `k` covers exactly
the close sites other than `k`.

**Theorem.** The binary search returns the maximum achievable minimum
distance.

*Proof.* Feasibility is monotone in `d`. By Lemmas 1 and 2 the 2-SAT instance
is satisfiable iff `d` is feasible, and 2-SAT is satisfiable iff no literal
shares a strongly connected component with its negation.

## Complexity and traps

`O(n log n log C)` with `C = 10^9`. Coinciding sites are within distance
`0 < d`. The two sites of one beacon may coincide, which must not create a
clause against itself. Recursive SCC overflows the stack, so use an iterative
Tarjan.

# 65. Temporal Steiner Span

## Union of root paths, minus the part above the LCA

Root the tree at `1`, and let each vertex own the cable to its parent. The
minimal connecting subgraph of the sites `l..r` is the union of their root
paths minus the root path of `LCA(l..r)`. Sweep `r` upward and paint the root
path of `r` with colour `r`. Then a cable lies on the root path of some site
in `[l, r]` iff its colour is at least `l`. A Fenwick tree over colours stores
the total cable length of each colour, so the union has length
`sum(colours >= l)`.

With heavy--light decomposition, every root path is a sequence of chain
**prefixes**. Each chain keeps a stack of equally coloured blocks from its
head downward. Painting a prefix pops fully covered blocks, trims one partial
block, and pushes the new block, each change updating the Fenwick tree.
`LCA(l..r)` is the LCA of the two sites with the smallest and largest DFS
entry time, found with sparse tables.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** After painting `1..r`, every cable's colour is the largest site
`<= r` whose root path contains it.

*Proof.* Painting in increasing order overwrites older colours.

**Lemma 2.** The union of the root paths of `l..r` minus the root path of their
LCA is the minimal connecting subgraph.

*Proof.* Every such root path passes through the LCA. The part above it is
used by no connecting path, and every cable below the LCA on a root path
separates some site from the LCA.

**Lemma 3.** The LCA of a vertex set is the LCA of its minimum and maximum DFS
entry times.

*Proof.* Both extremes lie in the LCA's subtree and in different child
subtrees (unless all sites share one), and every site lies between them in
DFS order.

**Theorem.** Each answer is the minimum lit length.

*Proof.* By Lemma 1 the Fenwick suffix gives the union's length, by Lemma 3
the depth of the correct LCA is subtracted, and Lemma 2 identifies the result.

## Complexity and traps

Each paint touches `O(log n)` chains, with amortized `O(1)` block changes per
chain, so the time is `O((n + q) log^2 n)` and the memory is `O(n log n)` for
the sparse tables. HLD LCA must compare the unweighted depths of chain heads,
not weighted depths. Sum cable lengths in 64 bits.
